records.name: Texas
records.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

sources.summary: Texas Tribune (12 Dec 2025): SB 8 implementation — DPS troopers ID-checked people at women's restrooms outside the Capitol on 6 Dec 2025 (trans women holding female ID markers were admitted), the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warn unclear guidelines produce uneven, invasive enforcement; protests followed at the Capitol.

Austin Current (27 Apr 2026): Attorney General Paxton's second complaint escalated the state probe of Austin ISD over bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint — the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry against a school district.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Texas carries the highest absolute toll of any state — 44 recorded killings of trans women 2008–2025, about 7.6 per 100k per year (undercount floor) — within the map's 'Do Not Travel' grading.

Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map, July 2026 update: Texas is one of four states in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers (with Florida, Idaho and Kansas), graded law-by-law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture by a five-year legislation-tracking methodology.

records.name: Tennessee
records.summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

sources.summary: LegalClarity (26 May 2026): the Adult Entertainment Act (2023, SB 3/HB 9) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — explicitly including 'male or female impersonators' — on public property or anywhere a child could see it; first offence is a Class A misdemeanour up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine, a second violation a Class E felony (1–6 years, fines to $3,000); it survived federal challenge on procedural grounds with a Supreme Court petition denied.

Advocate: the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to Tennessee's drag ban, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 Adult Entertainment Act in place; a separate suit remains ongoing, with performers saying they refuse to be silenced.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Tennessee's killing rate of trans women runs at 7.8 per 100k per year (10 recorded deaths, 2008–2025, undercount floor) and the state is graded in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier — the record's comparative-violence figure rests on this piece.

records.name: Kansas
records.summary: Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and voids state-issued IDs with corrected markers — licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified. The law also creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.

sources.summary: ACLU of Kansas SB 244 FAQ: the law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities with new civil and criminal penalties; bars updating driver's licences or state IDs and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex at birth — the Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Erin in the Morning legal-risk assessment (20 Feb 2026): Kansas escalated Worst Laws -> Do Not Travel — the first 'Do Not Travel' state added in a year — driven by the new bathroom-bounty law letting private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities; directly the assessment this record quotes on interstate-travel exposure.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HTTP 403); the underlying state-politics-news report covers two trans men who filed Doe v. State of Kansas within days of SB 244's enactment (late Feb 2026, ACLU and Ballard Spahr, Douglas County District Court), citing fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation law.

records.name: South Carolina
records.summary:
South Carolina's facility ban, enacted 2024, was expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities when the governor signed House Bill 4756 on May 15, 2026, requiring students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching sex assigned at birth.

The July 2026 assessment counts the expansion, raising the state's tier to 'Worst Laws Passed'; South Carolina is part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group and scores below the national score 0.36.

sources.summary: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: South Carolina is called out for expanding its bathroom ban to universities (campus settings added to the pre-existing restriction); the assessment's rubric ranks states on adult and youth law severity by reading bills, and South Carolina's expansion places it among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier.

ACLU of South Carolina (May 18, 2026): Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on Friday May 15, 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth; ACLU frames it as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education and notes the Senate amended the bill before passage. Press release dated May 18, 2026.
